title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper writes z := (λ0 − λ)/λ = sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)). The relativistic Doppler relation gives λ0/λ = 1+z = sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)), i.e. z = sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)) − 1. The stated equality is wrong, and it is inconsistent with the paper's own Eq. (5), β = ((1+z)²−1)/((1+z)²+1), and with Eqs. (11)–(12) where sqrt(1−β²)/(1−β) is set equal to (1+z), not z.

From the distance modulus Eq. (25), m − M = 5 log10(d_L/Mpc) + 25, one gets d_L = 10^((m−M−25)/5) Mpc. The paper writes d_L = 10^(m−M−25), omitting the division by 5; the exponent is wrong by a factor of 5.

Eq. (34) uses the Carroll–Press–Turner expression with (1+z)²(1+Ω_M z) − z(2+z)Ω_Λ, while Eq. (36) defines H(z′) := (1 + z′²)(1 + Ω_M z′) − z′Ω_Λ(2+z′). The factor (1 + z′²) should be (1 + z′)². The two equations, used interchangeably in Eqs. (35), (37), (39), (40), are mutually inconsistent.

The derivation v_i = dx_i/dτ = d(g_ik x^k)/dτ = (dg_ik/dτ)x^k + g_ik dx^k/dτ is invalid: coordinates x^k are not vector components, so g_ik x^k is not a covariant vector, and the four-velocity is u_i = g_ik u^k = g_ik dx^k/dτ, with no extra (dg_ik/dτ)x^k term. The conclusion drawn from it — that a comoving galaxy at fixed coordinates acquires an observed velocity merely because the metric evolves — is false (comoving observers have u^μ = (1,0,0,0) and zero peculiar velocity), yet it is the foundation of the whole paper.

Eq. (26) defines dS_O := r_O² dΩ_O, while Eq. (28) states dS_O = r_O²(1+z)² dΩ_O for the same symbol (the later text calls it dS′_O). Moreover, the factor is placed on the wrong side given the paper's own stated transformation ('the angle transformation law is still given by equations 12 and 18, but with swapped superscripts', i.e. dΩ_O = (1+z)² dΩ′): if the observed solid angle is LARGER by (1+z)², then for fixed proper size one must have dS_O (1+z)² = r_O² dΩ_O, giving d_A = r_O/(1+z), not d_A = r_O(1+z) as in Eq. (29). As written, Eq. (29) implies sources appear SMALLER, contradicting the preceding paragraph which argues they appear bigger.

The text says 'Substituting equations 21 and 28 in it [Eq. 30] and using the definitions ... we immediately obtain the Etherington relation'. Substituting dS_G = r_G² dΩ_G and dS_O = r_O²(1+z)² dΩ_O into dS_G dΩ_O = dS_O dΩ_G (1+z)² gives r_G = (1+z)² r_O, hence d_L = (1+z)² r_G = (1+z)^4 r_O while d_A = (1+z) r_O, so d_L/d_A = (1+z)³ ≠ (1+z)². The claimed recovery of Etherington's relation does not follow from the equations as written; it only works if the unmodified Eq. (26) is used, which contradicts the authors' own correction.

The claim that 'a small anisotropy will imply a solid angle 10^6 larger in our reference frame' applied to 'every point of the sky' is impossible: the total solid angle of the sky is fixed at 4π and aberration is a one-to-one remapping of directions, so it cannot magnify every patch by 10^6 nor 'mix' a patch with its neighbours. It also contradicts the paper's own Eq. (40), which gives d_A a factor (1+z) LARGER than the canonical angular diameter distance, i.e. angular sizes (1+z)² SMALLER, not larger.

The text invokes the existence of a minimum in the angular distance (Sandage 1961) to justify that larger apparent sizes do not mean closer objects, claiming this is 'in agreement with the correction'. But the paper's own Eq. (40), d_A = (c/H_0√|Ω_k|) F(√|Ω_k|∫dz′/√H), is monotonically increasing in z and has no maximum, so in the proposed model the angular-size turnover (a standard, observationally relevant prediction) disappears. The statement is therefore inconsistent with the derived result (and 'angular distance has a minimum' is itself a misstatement of the angular-size minimum / d_A maximum).

'Equation 5 clearly doesn't hold if the expansion of the Universe between us and the CO is faster than c, but in that case we simply can't detect any light signal from the CO so the problem doesn't arise.' This is factually wrong: in standard FLRW cosmology objects with recession velocities exceeding c (z ≳ 1.5) are routinely observed; superluminal recession does not prevent photons from reaching us. This also exposes the inconsistency of mapping cosmological redshift onto a special-relativistic β < 1.

The paper itself states that '(Ellis et al. 2012) also showed that usual Lorentz contraction and time dilation are contained in the FLRW metric'. If these effects are already contained in the metric, then Weinberg's derivation (in which the angle ε is already the solid angle subtended by the mirror as computed at the source along the null geodesics) already accounts for them, and multiplying the received flux by an extra (1+z)^-2 double counts the same physics. No independent demonstration is given that the standard FLRW result omits an aberration factor; the extra factor is simply appended.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 ('the age of Universe vary very little ... as shown in (Carroll et al. 1992)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Carroll, Press & Turner (1992) explicitly show that the dimensionless age H_0 t_0 varies strongly with Ω_M and Ω_Λ (from ~2/3 for Einstein–de Sitter to >1 for Λ-dominated models). The claim that the age depends 'strongly only on H_0' and varies 'very little' with the other cosmological parameters misrepresents the cited source and is false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3 ('temperature anisotropies of the CMB are in the order of 10^-6 K as measured in (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Planck measures ΔT/T ~ 10^-5, i.e. rms temperature anisotropies of order 10^-5 K (≈18 μK), not 10^-6 K. In addition, the 'interesting' juxtaposition of a dimensionless solid-angle magnification of 10^6 with a temperature in kelvin of 10^-6 is a meaningless numerological coincidence used to suggest physical significance.

The definition I_G := F_ν/dS′_O is inconsistent: I_G is supposed to be the (frequency-independent) surface brightness, while F_ν is the frequency-dependent flux density appearing on the left-hand side. Carrying the derivation through from Eq. (42) with dΩ_O = dS′_O/d_A² gives I_ν dν = (F_G/dS′_O) I(ν(1+z)) dν/(1+z)³, i.e. I_G := F_G/dS′_O.

Eq. (37) defines r_1 = F(√|Ω_k| ∫dz′/√H); for a flat universe (Ω_k = 0) the argument vanishes and F(x)=x yields r_1 = 0, so the expression is ill-defined/degenerate exactly in the case used on the RHS of Eq. (46), where r_1(z,0,Ω_Λ,can,Ω_M,can) is implicitly taken to be the plain integral ∫dz′/√H without the √|Ω_k| factor. The same symbol r_1 therefore denotes two different quantities in Eq. (46), and this inconsistency propagates to Eqs. (47)–(48).

The Friedmann-equation parametrisation underlying Eq. (34)/(36) (Carroll et al. 1992) implicitly imposes Ω_M + Ω_Λ + Ω_k = 1, so |Ω_k| > 1 would require Ω_M + Ω_Λ < 0 (negative total energy density) or > 2. The suggestion is made without acknowledging this constraint or the resulting unphysical implication, and without any quantitative fit.

'This article can be easily experimentally disproved if the correction proposed applied to the data analysis of a gravitational wave generated by two merging neutron stars will produce two measures of their original masses above the Volkov-Oppenheimer limit.' Component masses in compact-binary GW observations are determined from the phase evolution (chirp mass) and the independently measured redshift (e.g. from the EM counterpart of GW170817), not from the flux amplitude; a change in the d_L–z relation does not rescale the inferred source-frame masses in the way claimed, so the proposed falsification test is invalid. (The limit is also misnamed: it is the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit.)

Section 3.3 opens with 'It seems like the cosmological parameters observed through the CMB should be correct', whereas the Abstract and Conclusions state that the proposed correction changes the cosmological parameters measured 'from the CMB power spectrum analysis of the Plank Collaboration', and the same section later says CMB-derived parameters 'should be corrected and cleaned by this effect'. The paper asserts both that CMB parameters are correct and that they are wrong.

The apparent superluminal proper motion of jet components in 3C 279 is explained by geometric projection of a relativistic jet moving close to the line of sight (Rees 1966), not by replacing the classical Doppler formula with the relativistic one in the redshift–velocity conversion. Attributing the resolution of this problem to the relativistic Doppler formula of Eq. (5) conflates the recession velocity inferred from cosmological redshift with the transverse jet motion, and misrepresents the cited works.

The CMB dipole is produced by the Doppler boost of the observer's peculiar motion, and aberration from peculiar motion redistributes (couples) multipole power rather than simply 'increasing the intensity of high-order multipoles'. The characterisation of the cited literature, and the claim that the present effect is 'exactly the opposite' (a smoothing of anisotropies), misrepresents those works; aberration, being an invertible remapping of the sphere, cannot erase anisotropy.

The 'proof' offered for neglecting the acceleration of the expansion — 'the Hubble parameter nowadays is nearly a constant' — does not justify treating the observer and a high-redshift source (separated by billions of years of lookback time, over which H(z) changes by factors of several) as two inertial frames related by a global Lorentz transformation. This unjustified assumption is essential to every subsequent special-relativistic step.
